name: The Devils Club

waypoints.name: Ross Dam Trailhead (SR-20 milepost 134)
waypoints.note: US-side approach, opposite the Depot Creek approach used for the West Ridge/Beckey route. Climbers take a water taxi (or boat, portaging Diablo Lake to Ross Lake) up Ross Lake ~15 miles to the Little Beaver landing/dock, then hike/bushwhack up the Perry Creek drainage to reach the base of Southeast Mox Peak's East Face.
waypoints.directions: From Marblemount, drive SR-20 east past Newhalem and Diablo to the Ross Dam Trailhead near milepost 134, about 14 miles past Newhalem, and park in the small lot. From here a trail drops about 1 mile through forest toward Ross Dam; at the bottom, turn right on the gravel road to the lakeshore, where a phone on the last power pole calls Ross Lake Resort for the water taxi, which must be reserved in advance.

waypoints.name: Southeast Mox Peak (Hard Mox) summit / East Face high point

approach: Access starts on Ross Lake: from the Ross Dam trailhead on SR-20 (near milepost 134), hike the short Ross Dam Trail down to Ross Lake Resort, then take the resort's water taxi (or paddle a canoe) roughly 20+ miles up-lake to the Little Beaver Creek dock at the lake's north end. From the dock, follow the maintained (but lightly traveled) Little Beaver Trail west, paralleling Little Beaver Creek through cedar-fir forest with several brushy meadows and creek crossings, about 4.6-5 miles to Perry Creek Camp/Shelter, a three-sided log shelter that marks the effective end of maintained tread for climbers headed toward the Mox massif. From Perry Creek Camp there is no trail: the standard line follows the Perry Creek drainage south, and staying in or right beside the creekbed itself gives the fastest travel (easy rock-hopping and scrambling) up to about 3,600 ft, where dense slide alder chokes the creek and forces climbers up onto a bank. The south (true left) side of the drainage is preferred here — it holds older, more open forest and fewer avalanche paths, while the north side is a nearly impenetrable slide-alder thicket. Above the alder band the forest opens into blueberry meadows and sparser timber where travel speed improves to roughly 2-3 mph, eventually gaining the upper Perry Creek/Mox basin cirque below the connecting ridge to Southeast Mox, with talus and (season-dependent) snowfields and moats guarding the final approach to the toe of the 2,400-2,500 ft East Face. This is a genuinely serious approach, not a formality: the FA party (Layton/Wolfe, 2005) needed two full days in the rain from the lake to the base — 4.5 miles of trail, then roughly 14 hours of brush and creek travel up Perry Creek — and described it as one of the worst approaches in the Cascades. Expect cold creek fords, soaked gear, torn-up skin from devil's club and slide alder (the plant the route is named for), and real route-finding judgment calls about which side of the drainage to commit to. Water is abundant the entire way (Little Beaver Creek, Perry Creek) but should be treated.
